info.bio:
Tommy Dorsey (19 de noviembre de 1905 – 26 de noviembre de 1956), fue un trombonista de jazz y director de big band estadounidense.

Thomas Francis Dorsey, Jr. nació en Shenandoah, Pennsylvania, y comenzó su carrera musical a los 16 años en Pennsylvania oeste tocando en la big band "The Scranton Sirens", cubriendo el puesto que había dejado Russ Morgan.

scenes.name: Orquestas de baile: Whiteman y Goldkette
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Músicas «en los intersticios» que las historias del jazz desprecian. Jean Goldkette, más empresario que músico, reúne a Bix, Tram, Venuti, Lang, los Dorsey, Nichols y el arreglista Bill Challis: en 1926 barre a la banda de Fletcher Henderson en un duelo y Rex Stewart la llama «la primera banda blanca de swing». Paul Whiteman, autoproclamado «rey del jazz» (Robert Goffin dedica en 1931 su libro a «Louis Armstrong, el verdadero rey del jazz»), encarga la Rhapsody in Blue a Gershwin, vende millones con «Whispering» y arreglos pseudoclásicos, pero también da cabida a Bix, a los arreglos de Challis («Changes») y a Bing Crosby, que inventa el canto íntimo de la era del micrófono. Para Gioia, la pureza en la música es un mito.

scenes.name: Boogie-woogie
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Una mano izquierda insistente que repite patrones sobre los acordes del blues mientras la derecha sincopa melodías o acordes en bloque: exige independencia entre las manos. El nombre aparece a finales de los años veinte, quizá por un baile (lo sugiere el comentario de Pine Top Smith en su «Pine Top's Boogie Woogie»), y el estilo vive entre el blues y el jazz, sobre todo como piano solo o a dúos y tríos (Meade Lux Lewis, Albert Ammons, Pete Johnson). Hacia 1940 lo adoptan las grandes bandas de swing y hasta las Andrews Sisters.

scenes.name: Casa Loma, Dorsey, Shaw y Miller: las big bands blancas
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Antes de Goodman, la Casa Loma Orchestra (cooperativa salida de Goldkette, dirigida por Glen Gray, arreglos de Gene Gifford) conquista los campus con tempos frenéticos y secciones impecables: los jóvenes empiezan a dictar el gusto musical y la música se vuelve un «estilo de vida». Bob Crosby lleva el Dixieland a la big band; Tommy Dorsey, tras pelearse con su hermano Jimmy, acumula éxitos («Marie», «Song of India», un joven Frank Sinatra) y se vuelve más swing con Sy Oliver. Artie Shaw, «rey del clarinete», rival elegante y frío de Goodman, ocho veces casado, triunfa con «Begin the Beguine» y contrata a Billie Holiday y Roy Eldridge. Glenn Miller cierra el ciclo con riffs fáciles y melodías pegadizas («Moonlight Serenade», «In the Mood») que anuncian la música popular de posguerra. La huelga de Petrillo (1942-1944), la guerra y el propio agotamiento del swing acaban con la época más que el bebop.

Como ocurrió con la inyección de swing aportada por Henderson a la banda de Goodman, Oliver ayudó al grupo de Dorsey a convertirse en un conjunto más vivo y con un swing más potente. En los años siguientes, arreglos de Oliver como «Stomp It Off», «Yes, Indeed!», «Swing High», «Well, Get It!» y «Opus One» dieron un estilo más exuberante e insistente a la orquesta de Dorsey. podcast.title: Big Band Leader
podcast.body: Tommy Dorsey was a significant band leader during the Big Band era, leading large orchestras in which he was the central figure. His musicians and singers were employees, following his precise instructions. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinction from Thomas Dorsey
podcast.body: Mentioned to clarify that he is a different person from Thomas Dorsey, the inventor of gospel music, specifically a white bandleader. "This is not the same man as the white band leader Tommy Dorsey, who we've mentioned a couple of times earlier."

podcast.title: Host of "Stage Show"
podcast.body: Tommy Dorsey, a swing band-leader, co-presented the "Stage Show" TV program with Jimmy Dorsey, which was one of Elvis Presley's early television appearances. "a program that was presented by the swing band-leaders Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Impact of Musicians' Union Strike
podcast.body: Tommy Dorsey's band, as an instrumental ensemble on a major label, was unable to record any new music for two years during the Musicians' Union Strike of 1942-44 due to the dispute over royalties. However, his former vocalist, Frank Sinatra, could still record, backed by vocal groups. "Tommy Dorsi's band couldn't record anything, but Dorsi's old vocalist Frank Sinatra could, backed by a vocal group instead of instrumentalists."

xref.title: Big Band Leader
xref.body: Paul Whiteman was a prominent band leader during the Big Band era of jazz, leading large orchestras of ten or more musicians. These leaders were the stars, with all other musicians and singers functioning as employees under their rigid direction. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Big Band Leader
xref.body: Benny Goodman was recognized as a major band leader in the Big Band jazz scene. He directed large ensembles, and under the Big Band structure, all performers were subservient to the leader's artistic and musical authority. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Jazz Standards Repertoire
xref.body: As Jimmy Chamberlin's main gig from the age of 15, JP and the Cats played a repertoire rich in jazz standards. Their performances included works by renowned artists such as Benny Goodman, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, and Gene Krupa, connecting the group to the big band era of the 1930s and 1940s. "His main gig was with a group called JP and the Cats, lots of standards by Benny Goodman and Count Basie and Tommy Dorsey, Jean Crouppa, and many other legends of the 30s and 40s."

xref.title: Teenage Big Band Performer
xref.body: Jimmy Chamberlin demonstrated exceptional talent from a young age, starting to work in touring big bands when he was just 15. His primary engagement was with a group called JP and the Cats, where he performed numerous standards by legends such as Benny Goodman, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, and Gene Krupa, connecting him directly to the music of the 1930s and 1940s. "His main gig was with a group called JP and the Cats, lots of standards by Benny Goodman and Count Basie and Tommy Dorsey, Jean Crouppa, and many other legends of the 30s and 40s."
